7	## t001: fix: handle web stream payload in HEAD route
8	
9	Fixes #6371
10	
11	Issue #6371: HEAD route throws `ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE` error when GET route sends a Web Stream
12	
13	### Prerequisites
14	
15	- [x] I have written a descriptive issue title
16	- [x] I have searched existing issues to ensure the bug has not already been reported
17	
18	### Fastify version
19	
20	5.6.1
21	
22	### Plugin version
23	
24	_No response_
25	
26	### Node.js version
27	
28	22.18.0
29	
30	### Operating system
31	
32	macOS
33	
34	### Operating system version (i.e. 20.04, 11.3, 10)
35	
36	15.6
37	
38	### Description
39	
40	### Summary
41	Fastify automatically creates a corresponding `HEAD` route for every `GET` route. However, if the `GET` route handler sends a Web Stream (e.g., a `ReadableStream`), making a request to the `HEAD` route throws a `TypeError`.
42	
43	### Steps to Reproduce
44	1. Register a `GET` route that replies with a Web Stream payload (e.g., `new ReadableStream(...)`).
45	2. Start the Fastify server.
46	3. Send a `HEAD` request to the same route.
47	4. The server crashes with the error below.
48	
49	### Error Details
50	The following `TypeError` is thrown:
51	
52	```
53	TypeError [ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE]: The "string" argument must be of type string or an instance of Buffer or ArrayBuffer. Received an instance of ReadableStream
54	    at Function.byteLength (node:buffer:777:11)
55	    ...
56	```
57	
58	### Analysis
59	This error originates from the `headRouteOnSendHandler` function, specifically at this line:
60	
61	This line incorrectly assumes the payload is a Buffer-like type (`string`, `Buffer`, or `ArrayBuffer`, ...) to calculate the `Content-Length`.
62	Thus `Buffer.byteLength` fails causing the error when the payload is a `ReadableStream`.
63	
64	### Link to code that reproduces the bug
65	
66	https://github.com/orionmiz/fastify-repro-web-stream-in-head
67	
68	### Expected Behavior
69	
70	**HEAD request to a route whose corresponding GET handler sends a Web Stream should not throw an error.**
71	
72	- The `headRouteOnSendHandler` should not attempt to calculate the `Content-Length` of a stream payload (e.g., by calling `Buffer.byteLength`).
73	- Instead, in accordance with the HTTP specification, the `HEAD` response must include the exact same headers (such as `Transfer-Encoding` or `Content-Length`) that would have been sent by the corresponding `GET` request.
74	
75	You may update existing tests whose expectations your change intentionally alters.

265	## t002: fix: consistent error handling for custom validators in async validation contexts
266	
267	## Description
268	
269	Fixes inconsistent error handling between sync and async validation contexts when custom validators throw errors instead of returning `{error}` objects.
270	
271	## Problem
272	
273	When using async preValidation hooks with custom validators, if the validator throws an error (instead of returning `{error}`), the error would not be caught by the error handler and would result in an unhandled promise rejection, potentially crashing the application.
274	
275	This inconsistency meant:
276	- **Sync context**: Thrown errors were caught and handled properly by the error handler
277	- **Async context**: Thrown errors became unhandled promise rejections
278	
279	## Solution
280	
281	Modified the `validateParam` function in `lib/validation.js` to wrap the `validatorFunction` call in a try-catch block. This ensures that synchronous throws are caught and returned as validation errors, making error handling consistent across both sync and async validation contexts.
282	
283	## Changes
284	
285	- **lib/validation.js**: Added try-catch block around `validatorFunction` call in `validateParam`
286	- **test/validation-error-handling.test.js**: Added test case to verify error handling consistency
287	
288	## Testing
289	
290	- ✅ All existing tests pass
291	- ✅ New test specifically validates the fix for async preValidation + custom validator error scenarios
292	- ✅ Covers the exact issue described in #6214
293	
294	## Breaking Changes
295	
296	None. This change maintains backward compatibility while fixing the error handling inconsistency.
297	
298	Fixes #6214
299	
300	You may update existing tests whose expectations your change intentionally alters.

449	## t004: fix: set status code before publishing diagnostics error channel
450	
451	## Summary
452	
453	Fixes #6409
454	
455	Previously, the `tracing:fastify.request.handler:error` diagnostics channel would always report `reply.statusCode` as 200 because the channel was published before the error handler had a chance to set the appropriate status code.
456	
457	This fix sets the status code based on the error's `statusCode` or `status` property before publishing the diagnostics channel event, so subscribers can see the correct status code.
458	
459	## Changes
460	
461	- `lib/handle-request.js`: Set status code before publishing error channel (both sync error paths)
462	- `lib/wrap-thenable.js`: Set status code before publishing error channel (async error path)
463	- Added tests verifying the fix
464	
465	## Test plan
466	
467	- [x] Added test: `diagnostics channel error event should report correct status code` - verifies error with statusCode
468	- [x] Added test: `diagnostics channel error event should report 500 for errors without status` - verifies plain errors default to 500
469	- [x] Added test: `diagnostics channel error event should report correct status with custom error handler` - documents behavior with custom error handlers
470	- [x] All existing tests pass
471	
472	You may update existing tests whose expectations your change intentionally alters.

571	## t005: fix(ts): Align routerOptions defaultRoute types with runtime
572	
573	## Summary
574	
575	Fixes #6389.
576	
577	### What was broken
578	
579	`routerOptions.defaultRoute` and `routerOptions.onBadUrl` were typed as receiving `FastifyReply`, but the runtime always provides the raw Node `ServerResponse`. Consumers relying on the typed `FastifyReply` helpers (for example `reply.send`) hit runtime errors despite the compiler reporting everything as safe.
580	
581	### What this PR changes
582	
583	- retunes the TypeScript definitions for both callbacks to `RawRequestDefaultExpression`/`RawReplyDefaultExpression`, so the compiler finally describes what the runtime actually hands you
584	- calls out in `docs/Reference/Server.md` that these hooks get raw `IncomingMessage`/`ServerResponse` objects, setting expectations for folks writing plain JavaScript too
585	- drops a tsd regression in `test/types/instance.test-d.ts` so `routerOptions` can’t quietly drift back to exposing `FastifyReply`
586	
587	### Testing evidence
588	
589	- `npm run lint` → passes (eslint only)
590	- `npm run unit` → passes (borp, 2,140 tests run, 0 failures, 4 skips)
591	- `npm run test:typescript` → passes (tsc + tsd)
592	- `npm run benchmark --if-present` → passes (autocannon ~119k req/s avg, 672 MB read over 30 s)

614	function runBadClientCall (reqOptions, payload, waitBeforeDestroy) {
615	  let innerResolve, innerReject
616	  const promise = new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
617	    innerResolve = resolve
618	    innerReject = reject
619	  })
620	
621	  const postData = JSON.stringify(payload)
622

628	    }

630	    innerReject(new Error('Request should have failed'))
631	  })
632	
633	  // Kill the socket after the request has been fully written.
634	  // Destroying it on `connect` can race before any bytes are sent, making the
635	  // server-side assertions (hooks/handler) non-deterministic.
636	  //
637	  // To keep the test deterministic, we optionally wait for a server-side signal
638	  // (e.g. onSend entered) before aborting the client.
639	  let socket
640	  req.on('socket', (s) => { socket = s })
641	  req.on('finish', () => {
642	    if (waitBeforeDestroy && typeof waitBeforeDestroy.then === 'function') {
643	      Promise.race([
644	        waitBeforeDestroy,
645	        new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 200))
646	      ]).then(() => {
647	        if (socket) socket.destroy()
648	      }, innerResolve)
649	      return
650	    }
651	    setTimeout(() => { socket.destroy() }, 0)
652	  })
653	  req.on('error', innerResolve)
654	  req.write(postData)
655	  req.end()
656	
657	  return promise
658	}

992	## t007: chore: Updated content-type header parsing
993	
994	Resolves #6332.
995	
996	This is a follow-on from #6303. This introduces a more robust content-type header value parsing algorithm.
997	
998	***IMPORTANT:*** this results in much stricter content-type handling. Prior to this PR, we were accepting, and handling, headers like `content-type: a-simple-string`. That is not valid. 1000	This change _also_ enforces normalization of the content-type value. For example, if the request has `application/json; charset=utf-8` as the value, it will be normalized to `application/json; charset="utf-8"`.

996	This is a follow-on from #6303. This introduces a more robust content-type header value parsing algorithm.

998	***IMPORTANT:*** this results in much stricter content-type handling. Prior to this PR, we were accepting, and handling, headers like `content-type: a-simple-string`. That is not valid. There must be a type **and** a subtype present. So a "valid" form would be `content-type: a-simple-string/foo`.
999	
1000	This change _also_ enforces normalization of the content-type value. For example, if the request has `application/json; charset=utf-8` as the value, it will be normalized to `application/json; charset="utf-8"`.
1001

1768	## t008: fix: avoid mutating shared routerOptions across instances
1769	
1770	## Problem
1771	
1772	Reusing the same `routerOptions` object across multiple Fastify instances can fail with:
1773	
1774	`TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'server')`
1775	
1776	`buildRouterOptions()` was mutating the user-provided `options.routerOptions` object in place while filling defaults (including instance-bound callbacks like `defaultRoute` / `onBadUrl`).
1777	
1778	## Fix
1779	
1780	- clone `options.routerOptions` before filling defaults
1781	- avoid mutating user-provided config objects

1786	- add regression test: `Should not mutate user-provided routerOptions object`
1787	- ensure cleanup uses `t.after()` so instances are always closed
1788	
1789	Fixes #6512

1870	## t009: feat: First-class support for handler-level timeouts
1871	
1872	Adds a first-class handlerTimeout option, configurable per-server and per-route, backed by an AbortSignal exposed as request.signal. Unlike the existing socket-level timeouts (connectionTimeout, requestTimeout), this is an application-level timeout that works correctly with HTTP keep-alive and can be scoped to individual routes, and used together with flows that support AbortSignal (fetch, DBs etc).
1873	
1874	  Highlights
1875	
1876	  - Zero overhead when disabled: default is 0 (no timeout). No AbortController, setTimeout, or event listeners are
1877	  created, only a single branch check per request
1878	  - Per-route override: works like bodyLimit — routes inherit the server default and can override with a different
1879	  value;
1880	  - Cooperative cancellation: timeout sends a 503 response and aborts request.signal, but does not kill the handler.
1881	  Handlers use request.signal to propagate cancellation to downstream I/O;
1882	  - Unified signal: request.signal aborts on either timeout or client disconnect. signal.reason distinguishes the two
1883	  (FST_ERR_HANDLER_TIMEOUT vs generic AbortError);
1884	  - Full resource cleanup: timer and close listener are cleaned up in every exit path — normal response, error,
1885	  reply.hijack(), timeout, and client disconnect;
1886	  - Customizable error response: the timeout error flows through the route's errorHandler, allowing per-route
1887	  status/body customization;
1888	  - Fail-fast on misconfiguration: accessing request.signal without handlerTimeout configured throws
1889	  FST_ERR_MISSING_HANDLER_TIMEOUT.
1890

265	## t002: fix: consistent error handling for custom validators in async validation contexts
266	
267	## Description
268	
269	Fixes inconsistent error handling between sync and async validation contexts when custom validators throw errors instead of returning `{error}` objects.
270	
271	## Problem
272	
273	When using async preValidation hooks with custom validators, if the validator throws an error (instead of returning `{error}`), the error would not be caught by the error handler and would result in an unhandled promise rejection, potentially crashing the application.
274	
275	This inconsistency meant:
276	- **Sync context**: Thrown errors were caught and handled properly by the error handler
277	- **Async context**: Thrown errors became unhandled promise rejections
278	
279	## Solution
280	
281	Modified the `validateParam` function in `lib/validation.js` to wrap the `validatorFunction` call in a try-catch block. This ensures that synchronous throws are caught and returned as validation errors, making error handling consistent across both sync and async validation contexts.
282	
283	## Changes
284	
285	- **lib/validation.js**: Added try-catch block around `validatorFunction` call in `validateParam`
286	- **test/validation-error-handling.test.js**: Added test case to verify error handling consistency
287	
288	## Testing
289	
290	- ✅ All existing tests pass
291	- ✅ New test specifically validates the fix for async preValidation + custom validator error scenarios
292	- ✅ Covers the exact issue described in #6214
293	
294	## Breaking Changes
295	
296	None. This change maintains backward compatibility while fixing the error handling inconsistency.
297	
298	Fixes #6214
299	
300	You may update existing tests whose expectations your change intentionally alters.
301	
302	Acceptance tests:
303	
304	`test/validation-error-handling.pr6247.test.js`
305	
306	```js
307	'use strict'
308	
309	const { describe, test } = require('node:test')
310	const Joi = require('joi')
311	const Fastify = require('..')
312	
313	const schema = {
314	  body: {
315	    type: 'object',
316	    properties: {
317	      name: { type: 'string' },
318	      work: { type: 'string' }
319	    },
320	    required: ['name', 'work']
321	  }
322	}
323	
324	function echoBody (req, reply) {
325	  reply.code(200).send(req.body.name)
326	}
327	
328	describe('sync and async must work in the same way', () => {
329	  // Route with custom validator that throws
330	  const throwingRouteValidator = {
331	    schema: {
332	      body: {
333	        type: 'object',
334	        properties: { name: { type: 'string' } }
335	      }
336	    },
337	    validatorCompiler: () => {
338	      return function (inputData) {
339	        // This custom validator throws a sync error instead of returning `{ error }`
340	        throw new Error('Custom validation failed')
341	      }
342	    },
343	    handler (request, reply) { reply.send({ success: true }) }
344	  }
345	
346	  test('async preValidation with custom validator should trigger error handler when validator throws', async (t) => {
347	    t.plan(4)
348	
349	    const fastify = Fastify()
350	    fastify.setErrorHandler((error, request, reply) => {
351	      t.assert.ok(error instanceof Error, 'error should be an Error instance')
352	      t.assert.strictEqual(error.message, 'Custom validation failed')
353	      reply.status(500).send({ error: error.message })
354	    })
355	
356	    // Add async preValidation hook
357	    fastify.addHook('preValidation', async (request, reply) => {
358	      await Promise.resolve('ok')
359	    })
360	    fastify.post('/async', throwingRouteValidator)
361	
362	    const response = await fastify.inject({
363	      method: 'POST',
364	      url: '/async',
365	      payload: { name: 'test' }
366	    })
367	    t.assert.strictEqual(response.statusCode, 500)
368	    t.assert.deepStrictEqual(response.json(), { error: 'Custom validation failed' })
369	  })
370	
371	  test('sync preValidation with custom validator should trigger error handler when validator throws', async (t) => {
372	    t.plan(4)
373	
374	    const fastify = Fastify()
375	    fastify.setErrorHandler((error, request, reply) => {
376	      t.assert.ok(error instanceof Error, 'error should be an Error instance')
377	      t.assert.strictEqual(error.message, 'Custom validation failed')
378	      reply.status(500).send({ error: error.message })
379	    })
380	
381	    // Add sync preValidation hook
382	    fastify.addHook('preValidation', (request, reply, next) => { next() })
383	    fastify.post('/sync', throwingRouteValidator)
384	
385	    const response = await fastify.inject({
386	      method: 'POST',
387	      url: '/sync',
388	      payload: { name: 'test' }
389	    })
390	    t.assert.strictEqual(response.statusCode, 500)
391	    t.assert.deepStrictEqual(response.json(), { error: 'Custom validation failed' })
392	  })
393	})
394	```

450	
451	## Summary
452	
453	Fixes #6409
454	
455	Previously, the `tracing:fastify.request.handler:error` diagnostics channel would always report `reply.statusCode` as 200 because the channel was published before the error handler had a chance to set the appropriate status code.
456	
457	This fix sets the status code based on the error's `statusCode` or `status` property before publishing the diagnostics channel event, so subscribers can see the correct status code.

3861	## t024: fix: avoid double slash when joining nested prefixes
3862	
3863	## What
3864	
3865	`buildRoutePrefix` joins a parent register's prefix with a child register's
3866	prefix and is meant to keep exactly one `/` between them (per the existing
3867	`'/first//second'` comment). It misses the case where the parent prefix ends
3868	with `/` and the child prefix has no leading `/`: it prepends a `/` anyway and
3869	produces a double slash.
3870	
3871	For example:
3872	
3873	```js
3874	fastify.register(function (instance, opts, done) {
3875	  instance.register(function (sub, opts, done) {
3876	    sub.get('/route', handler)
3877	    done()
3878	  }, { prefix: 'inner' })   // no leading slash
3879	  done()
3880	}, { prefix: '/v1/' })      // trailing slash
3881	```
3882	
3883	registers the route at `/v1//inner/route` instead of `/v1/inner/route`. With the
3884	default `ignoreDuplicateSlashes: false`, `GET /v1/inner/route` then returns 404.
3885	
3886	## How
3887	
3888	Only prepend the separating `/` when the parent prefix does not already end with
3889	one. This matches the existing route-path handling in `lib/route.js` ("Ensure
3890	that '/prefix/' + '/route' gets registered as '/prefix/route'").
3891	
3892	## Testing
3893	
3894	Added a test in `test/route-prefix.test.js` for a trailing-slash parent prefix
3895	combined with a no-leading-slash child prefix. It fails before the change and
3896	passes after. Lint, the full unit suite, type tests, and the 100% coverage check
3897	pass locally.

3947	## t025: fix: hasRequestDecorator/hasReplyDecorator misses constructor-assigned built-in properties
3948	
3949	## What
3950	
3951	`hasRequestDecorator` and `hasReplyDecorator` only check the constructor prototype and the decorator props list. But several core properties — `req.id`, `req.params`, `req.raw`, `req.query`, `req.log`, `req.body`, `reply.raw`, `reply.request`, `reply.log` — are assigned directly in the `Request` and `Reply` constructors, not on their prototypes.
3952	
3953	This means:
3954	
3955	```js
3956	fastify.hasRequestDecorator('id')   // returns false (wrong)
3957	fastify.decorateRequest('id', null) // silently succeeds (wrong)
3958	// then at request time:
3959	// TypeError: Cannot set property id... or req.id is null
3960	```
3961	
3962	## Root cause
3963	
3964	`checkRequestExistence` and `decorateConstructor` in `lib/decorate.js` use `Object.hasOwn(prototype, name)` and `name in prototype`. Properties set in the constructor body are never on the prototype, so these checks miss them.
3965	
3966	## Fix
3967	
3968	Add an `instanceProperties` set to `Request` and `Reply` listing their constructor-assigned string-keyed properties. `decorateConstructor` and the `checkRequest/ReplyExistence` helpers now also check this set (walking the parent chain for derived constructors).
3969	
3970	After the fix:
3971	
3972	```js
3973	fastify.hasRequestDecorator('id')     // true
3974	fastify.hasReplyDecorator('raw')      // true
3975	fastify.decorateRequest('id', null)   // throws FST_ERR_DEC_ALREADY_PRESENT
3976	fastify.decorateReply('raw', null)    // throws FST_ERR_DEC_ALREADY_PRESENT
3977	fastify.decorateRequest('myExtra', null) // still works fine
3978	```
3979	
3980	All 52 existing decorator tests pass. Six new node:test tests cover the bug and the fix.
3981	
3982	You may update existing tests whose expectations your change intentionally alters.
3983

4806	## t031: fix: recognize constructor-assigned built-in properties as decorator …
4807	
4808	## Summary
4809	
4810	`decorate*`'s `dependencies` option rejects the built-in `Request`/`Reply`
4811	properties that are assigned in the constructor, even though every other
4812	decorator API treats them as present. Fastify currently gives two different
4813	answers for the same name:
4814	
4815	```js
4816	const fastify = Fastify()
4817	
4818	fastify.hasRequestDecorator('body')          // true
4819	fastify.decorateRequest('body', fn)          // FST_ERR_DEC_ALREADY_PRESENT
4820	fastify.decorateRequest('x', fn, ['body'])   // FST_ERR_DEC_MISSING_DEPENDENCY
4821	```
4822	
4823	A decorator cannot declare `body`, `id`, `params`, `query`, `log` or `raw` as
4824	a dependency, while at the same time it cannot decorate over them and
4825	`hasRequestDecorator` reports them as present. The same applies to `raw`,
4826	`request` and `log` on `Reply`.
4827	
4828	## Root cause
4829	
4830	Follow-up to #6753.
4831	
4832	#6753 introduced `hasInstanceProperty` to make Fastify aware of properties
4833	assigned in the `Request`/`Reply` constructors rather than defined on the
4834	prototype. It was wired into three call sites: the
4835	`FST_ERR_DEC_ALREADY_PRESENT` guard in `decorateConstructor`,
4836	`checkRequestExistence` and `checkReplyExistence`.
4837	
4838	The dependency check was not updated. It still resolves names through
4839	`checkExistence` alone, which only looks at the instance, its prototype and
4840	`props`, so constructor-assigned properties fall through and are reported as
4841	missing.
4842	
4843	## Solution
4844	
4845	`checkDependencies` now falls back to `hasInstanceProperty` when
4846	`checkExistence` does not find a dependency.
4847	
4848	The instance path is unaffected: `decorate()` passes a plain Fastify
4849	instance, which has no `instanceProperties`, so the lookup returns `false`
4850	immediately. The order also keeps the common case unchanged — for ordinary
4851	decorator dependencies `checkExistence` succeeds and the second lookup is
4852	never reached.
4853	
4854	## Tests
4855	
4856	Added to `test/decorator-instance-properties.test.js`:
4857	
4858	- the full built-in sets for both `Request` and `Reply` accepted as
4859	  dependencies
4860	- an encapsulated plugin, to exercise the `parent` chain
4861	- a dependency array mixing built-ins with user decorators
4862	- a regression test asserting that unknown dependencies still throw
4863	  `FST_ERR_DEC_MISSING_DEPENDENCY`, and that a `Reply` decorator depending on
4864	  a `Request`-only property still throws
4865	
4866	All four new cases fail on the base commit and pass with the change. Full
4867	suite, lint and type tests are green.
4868	
4869	You may update existing tests whose expectations your change intentionally alters.
4870	
4871	Acceptance tests:
4872	
4873	`test/decorator-instance-properties.pr6892.test.js`
4874	
4875	```js
4876	'use strict'
4877	
4878	const { test } = require('node:test')
4879	const Fastify = require('..')
4880	
4881	test('decorateRequest accepts built-in request properties as dependencies', t => {
4882	  t.plan(6)
4883	  const fastify = Fastify()
4884	  for (const name of ['id', 'params', 'raw', 'query', 'log', 'body']) {

38	### Description
39	
40	### Summary
41	Fastify automatically creates a corresponding `HEAD` route for every `GET` route. However, if the `GET` route handler sends a Web Stream (e.g., a `ReadableStream`), making a request to the `HEAD` route throws a `TypeError`.
42	
43	### Steps to Reproduce
44	1. Register a `GET` route that replies with a Web Stream payload (e.g., `new ReadableStream(...)`).
45	2. Start the Fastify server.
46	3. Send a `HEAD` request to the same route.
47	4. The server crashes with the error below.
48	
49	### Error Details
50	The following `TypeError` is thrown:
51	
52	```
53	TypeError [ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE]: The "string" argument must be of type string or an instance of Buffer or ArrayBuffer. Received an instance of ReadableStream
54	    at Function.byteLength (node:buffer:777:11)
55	    ...
56	```
57	
58	### Analysis
59	This error originates from the `headRouteOnSendHandler` function, specifically at this line:
60	
61	This line incorrectly assumes the payload is a Buffer-like type (`string`, `Buffer`, or `ArrayBuffer`, ...) to calculate the `Content-Length`.
62	Thus `Buffer.byteLength` fails causing the error when the payload is a `ReadableStream`.
63	
64	### Link to code that reproduces the bug
65	
66	https://github.com/orionmiz/fastify-repro-web-stream-in-head
67	
68	### Expected Behavior
69	
70	**HEAD request to a route whose corresponding GET handler sends a Web Stream should not throw an error.**
71	
72	- The `headRouteOnSendHandler` should not attempt to calculate the `Content-Length` of a stream payload (e.g., by calling `Buffer.byteLength`).
73	- Instead, in accordance with the HTTP specification, the `HEAD` response must include the exact same headers (such as `Transfer-Encoding` or `Content-Length`) that would have been sent by the corresponding `GET` request.

265	## t002: fix: consistent error handling for custom validators in async validation contexts
266	
267	## Description
268	
269	Fixes inconsistent error handling between sync and async validation contexts when custom validators throw errors instead of returning `{error}` objects.
270	
271	## Problem
272	
273	When using async preValidation hooks with custom validators, if the validator throws an error (instead of returning `{error}`), the error would not be caught by the error handler and would result in an unhandled promise rejection, potentially crashing the application.
274	
275	This inconsistency meant:
276	- **Sync context**: Thrown errors were caught and handled properly by the error handler
277	- **Async context**: Thrown errors became unhandled promise rejections
278	
279	## Solution
280	
281	Modified the `validateParam` function in `lib/validation.js` to wrap the `validatorFunction` call in a try-catch block. This ensures that synchronous throws are caught and returned as validation errors, making error handling consistent across both sync and async validation contexts.
282	
283	## Changes
284	
285	- **lib/validation.js**: Added try-catch block around `validatorFunction` call in `validateParam`
286	- **test/validation-error-handling.test.js**: Added test case to verify error handling consistency
287	
288	## Testing
289	
290	- ✅ All existing tests pass
291	- ✅ New test specifically validates the fix for async preValidation + custom validator error scenarios
292	- ✅ Covers the exact issue described in #6214
293	
294	## Breaking Changes
295	
296	None. This change maintains backward compatibility while fixing the error handling inconsistency.
297	
298	Fixes #6214

449	## t004: fix: set status code before publishing diagnostics error channel
450	
451	## Summary
452	
453	Fixes #6409
454	
455	Previously, the `tracing:fastify.request.handler:error` diagnostics channel would always report `reply.statusCode` as 200 because the channel was published before the error handler had a chance to set the appropriate status code.
456	
457	This fix sets the status code based on the error's `statusCode` or `status` property before publishing the diagnostics channel event, so subscribers can see the correct status code.
458	
459	## Changes
460	
461	- `lib/handle-request.js`: Set status code before publishing error channel (both sync error paths)
462	- `lib/wrap-thenable.js`: Set status code before publishing error channel (async error path)

4417	- Update `validateParam` when a custom validator returns an explicit `value`, including falsy values such as `0`, `""`, `false`, and `null`.

1870	## t009: feat: First-class support for handler-level timeouts
1871	
1872	Adds a first-class handlerTimeout option, configurable per-server and per-route, backed by an AbortSignal exposed as request.signal. Unlike the existing socket-level timeouts (connectionTimeout, requestTimeout), this is an application-level timeout that works correctly with HTTP keep-alive and can be scoped to individual routes, and used together with flows that support AbortSignal (fetch, DBs etc).
1873	
1874	  Highlights
1875	
1876	  - Zero overhead when disabled: default is 0 (no timeout). No AbortController, setTimeout, or event listeners are
1877	  created, only a single branch check per request
1878	  - Per-route override: works like bodyLimit — routes inherit the server default and can override with a different
1879	  value;
1880	  - Cooperative cancellation: timeout sends a 503 response and aborts request.signal, but does not kill the handler.
1881	  Handlers use request.signal to propagate cancellation to downstream I/O;
1882	  - Unified signal: request.signal aborts on either timeout or client disconnect. signal.reason distinguishes the two
1883	  (FST_ERR_HANDLER_TIMEOUT vs generic AbortError);
1884	  - Full resource cleanup: timer and close listener are cleaned up in every exit path — normal response, error,
1885	  reply.hijack(), timeout, and client disconnect;
1886	  - Customizable error response: the timeout error flows through the route's errorHandler, allowing per-route
1887	  status/body customization;
1888	  - Fail-fast on misconfiguration: accessing request.signal without handlerTimeout configured throws
1889	  FST_ERR_MISSING_HANDLER_TIMEOUT.

4054	## t026: fix: derive request.port from request.host
4055	
4056	This restores `request.port` to use the same effective host source as `request.host`.
4057	
4058	`#6603` fixed port parsing, but it also changed `request.port` to read directly from `request.headers.host` / `:authority`. When `trustProxy` is enabled, `request.host` may come from `x-forwarded-host`, so `request.host`, `request.hostname`, and `request.port` could disagree.
4059	
4060	This patch keeps the parsing logic from `#6603`, but parses from `request.host` so the three properties stay aligned again.
4061	
4062	It also adds coverage for the trust-proxy cases discussed in `#6671`, including `:authority` fallback.

5174	## t035: fix: callNotFound should run not-found preHandler regardless of registration order
5175	
5176	setContext() in four-oh-four.js takes a detached shallow snapshot of the
5177	selected not-found context. When a route that calls reply.callNotFound()
5178	is registered before setNotFoundHandler(), the snapshot is taken before
5179	the not-found handler's preReady callback populates its lifecycle hooks,
5180	so the copied context retains preHandler: null. reply.callNotFound() then

4984	## t033: fix: run preClose hook exactly once per declaring instance
4985	
4986	## What
4987	
4988	A single `preClose` hook added to a Fastify instance is executed once for **every** instance in the encapsulation subtree (the declaring instance plus each descendant plugin) instead of exactly once.
4989	
4990	### Reproduction
4991	
4992	```js
4993	const fastify = Fastify()
4994	let count = 0
4995	
4996	fastify.register(async (child) => {
4997	  child.get('/x', async () => 'ok')
4998	})
4999	fastify.addHook('preClose', async () => { count++ })
5000	
5001	await fastify.ready()
5002	await fastify.close()
5003	
5004	console.log(count) // 2, expected 1
5005	```
5006	
5007	With two levels of nested plugins the same hook runs 3 times. An equivalent `onReady` hook in the identical setup correctly runs once.
5008	
5009	### Root cause
5010	
5011	In `addHook`, the hooks `onReady`, `onListen`, and `onRoute` are special-cased to be stored only on the declaring instance via `this[kHooks].add`. `preClose` was omitted from that list, so it falls into the `else` branch and goes through `_addHook`, which copies the hook into every child via `this[kChildren].forEach`. At close time, `hookRunnerApplication('preClose')` already walks the entire child tree, so each propagated copy fires again.
5012	
5013	That `preClose` is not meant to be inherited is already established elsewhere in the codebase: `buildHooks` in `lib/hooks.js` resets `onReady`, `onListen`, and `preClose` to empty arrays for children. `preClose` was simply left off the special-case list in `addHook`.
5014	
5015	### Fix
5016	
5017	Add `preClose` to the same special-case branch as `onReady`/`onListen`/`onRoute` so it is stored only on the declaring instance and not propagated into children. Since `hookRunnerApplication` already recurses the child tree and `buildHooks` already excludes `preClose` from inheritance, each declared hook now fires exactly once.
5018	
5019	### Tests
5020	
5021	Added two regression tests in `test/close.test.js` (a single child plugin and nested child plugins) asserting the hook runs exactly once. Both fail on `main` (count 2 and 3) and pass with this change. The full `test/close.test.js` suite (26 tests) stays green.
5022	
5023	You may update existing tests whose expectations your change intentionally alters.
5024	
5025	Acceptance tests:
5026	
5027	`test/close.pr6940.test.js`
5028	
5029	```js

5038	const { sleep } = require('./helper')
5039	
5040	const server = http.createServer()
5041	const noSupport = typeof server.closeAllConnections !== 'function'
5042	
5043	test('preClose runs exactly once with a child plugin', async t => {
5044	  t.plan(1)
5045	  const fastify = Fastify()
5046	  let count = 0
5047	
5048	  fastify.register(async (child) => {
5049	    child.get('/x', async () => 'ok')
5050	  })
5051	  fastify.addHook('preClose', async () => { count++ })
5052	
5053	  await fastify.ready()
5054	  await fastify.close()
5055

5057	})

571	## t005: fix(ts): Align routerOptions defaultRoute types with runtime
572	
573	## Summary
574	
575	Fixes #6389.
576	
577	### What was broken
578	
579	`routerOptions.defaultRoute` and `routerOptions.onBadUrl` were typed as receiving `FastifyReply`, but the runtime always provides the raw Node `ServerResponse`. Consumers relying on the typed `FastifyReply` helpers (for example `reply.send`) hit runtime errors despite the compiler reporting everything as safe.
580	
581	### What this PR changes
582	
583	- retunes the TypeScript definitions for both callbacks to `RawRequestDefaultExpression`/`RawReplyDefaultExpression`, so the compiler finally describes what the runtime actually hands you
584	- calls out in `docs/Reference/Server.md` that these hooks get raw `IncomingMessage`/`ServerResponse` objects, setting expectations for folks writing plain JavaScript too
585	- drops a tsd regression in `test/types/instance.test-d.ts` so `routerOptions` can’t quietly drift back to exposing `FastifyReply`
586	
587	### Testing evidence
588	
589	- `npm run lint` → passes (eslint only)
590	- `npm run unit` → passes (borp, 2,140 tests run, 0 failures, 4 skips)
591	- `npm run test:typescript` → passes (tsc + tsd)
592	- `npm run benchmark --if-present` → passes (autocannon ~119k req/s avg, 672 MB read over 30 s)
593	
594	You may update existing tests whose expectations your change intentionally alters.
595	
596	Acceptance tests:
597	
598	`test/issue-4959.pr6392.test.js`
599	
600	```js
601	'use strict'
602	
603	const { test } = require('node:test')
604	const http = require('node:http')
605	const Fastify = require('../fastify')
606	const { setTimeout } = require('node:timers')
607	
608	/*
609	* Ensure that a socket error during the request does not cause the
610	* onSend hook to be called multiple times.
611	*
612	* @see https://github.com/fastify/fastify/issues/4959
613	*/
614	function runBadClientCall (reqOptions, payload, waitBeforeDestroy) {
615	  let innerResolve, innerReject
616	  const promise = new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
617	    innerResolve = resolve
618	    innerReject = reject
619	  })
620	
621	  const postData = JSON.stringify(payload)
622	
623	  const req = http.request({
624	    ...reqOptions,
625	    headers: {
626	      'Content-Type': 'application/json',
627	      'Content-Length': Buffer.byteLength(postData)
628	    }
629	  }, () => {
630	    innerReject(new Error('Request should have failed'))
631	  })
632	
633	  // Kill the socket after the request has been fully written.
634	  // Destroying it on `connect` can race before any bytes are sent, making the
635	  // server-side assertions (hooks/handler) non-deterministic.
636	  //
637	  // To keep the test deterministic, we optionally wait for a server-side signal
638	  // (e.g. onSend entered) before aborting the client.
639	  let socket
640	  req.on('socket', (s) => { socket = s })
641	  req.on('finish', () => {
642	    if (waitBeforeDestroy && typeof waitBeforeDestroy.then === 'function') {
643	      Promise.race([
644	        waitBeforeDestroy,
645	        new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 200))
646	      ]).then(() => {
647	        if (socket) socket.destroy()
648	      }, innerResolve)
649	      return
650	    }
651	    setTimeout(() => { socket.destroy() }, 0)
652	  })
653	  req.on('error', innerResolve)
654	  req.write(postData)
655	  req.end()
656	
657	  return promise
658	}
659	
660	test('should handle a socket error', async (t) => {
661	  t.plan(4)
662	  const fastify = Fastify()
663	
664	  let resolveOnSendEntered
665	  const onSendEntered = new Promise((resolve) => {
666	    resolveOnSendEntered = resolve
667	  })
668	
669	  function shouldNotHappen () {
670	    t.assert.fail('This should not happen')
671	  }
672	  process.on('unhandledRejection', shouldNotHappen)
673	
674	  t.after(() => {
675	    fastify.close()
676	    process.removeListener('unhandledRejection', shouldNotHappen)
677	  })
678	
679	  fastify.addHook('onRequest', async (request, reply) => {
680	    t.assert.ok('onRequest hook called')
681	  })
682	
683	  fastify.addHook('onSend', async (request, reply, payload) => {
684	    if (request.onSendCalled) {
685	      t.assert.fail('onSend hook called more than once')
686	      return
687	    }
688	
689	    t.assert.ok('onSend hook called')
690	    request.onSendCalled = true
691	
692	    if (resolveOnSendEntered) {
693	      resolveOnSendEntered()
694	      resolveOnSendEntered = null
695	    }
696	
697	    // Introduce a delay (gives time for client-side abort to happen while the
698	    // request has already been processed, exercising the original issue).
699	    await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 50))
700	    return payload
701	  })
702	
703	  // The handler must be async to trigger the error
704	  fastify.put('/', async (request, reply) => {
705	    t.assert.ok('PUT handler called')
706	    return reply.send({ hello: 'world' })
707	  })
708	
709	  await fastify.listen({ port: 0 })
710	
711	  const err = await runBadClientCall({
712	    hostname: 'localhost',
713	    port: fastify.server.address().port,
714	    path: '/',
715	    method: 'PUT'
716	  }, { test: 'me' }, onSendEntered)
717	  t.assert.equal(err.code, 'ECONNRESET')
718	})
719	```

725	
726	const split = require('split2')

731	  FST_ERR_BAD_URL,
732	  FST_ERR_ASYNC_CONSTRAINT
733	} = require('../lib/errors')
734	
735	test('Should support extra find-my-way options', async t => {
736	  t.plan(1)

738	  const fastify = Fastify({
739	    routerOptions: {

741	        const cleanMeta = Object.assign({}, route.store)
742	        return cleanMeta
743	      }
744	    }
745	  })
746	
747	  await fastify.ready()
748	
749	  // Ensure the option is preserved after validation
750	  t.assert.strictEqual(typeof fastify.initialConfig.routerOptions.buildPrettyMeta, 'function')
751	})
752	```

5681	## t037: perf: decode string bodies once instead of per chunk
5682	
5683	For string parsers, including the default JSON parser, `rawBody` called `setEncoding('utf8')`. On every request that meant:
5684	
5685	- a new StringDecoder,
5686	- decoding each chunk separately,
5687	- building the body with `body += chunk`,
5688	- running `Buffer.byteLength()` over every decoded chunk just to enforce `bodyLimit`.
5689	
5690	On a JSON POST profile this came to about 6% of busy CPU, more than routing, validation and hooks combined.
5691	
5692	This PR always reads raw Buffers and counts bytes with `chunk.length`. String bodies are decoded once at the end, with no copy when the body arrived in a single chunk. Buffer parsers still receive a `Buffer.concat` copy, so they never get a view over the shared socket read buffer. String chunks from a custom `preParsing` stream are converted with `Buffer.from`.
5693	
5694	### Bug fix
5695	
5696	The limit and `Content-Length` checks used to count bytes after decoding. An invalid UTF-8 byte decodes to U+FFFD, which is 3 bytes when counted again. So a body with the correct `Content-Length` was rejected with `FST_ERR_CTP_INVALID_CONTENT_LENGTH`. Both checks now count the bytes actually received.
5697

4643	## t030: fix: clear trailer state when removing all trailers
4644	
4645	### Description
4646	
4647	`reply.removeTrailer()` marked removed trailers as `undefined`, but it did not clear the internal trailer state when all active trailer callbacks were removed.
4648	
4649	Because the send path checks whether trailer state is non-null, a response could still enter trailer mode after all trailers were removed. That could produce chunked framing, an empty `Trailer` header, and no `Content-Length` even though no trailers remained.
4650	
4651	This change clears the trailer state when no active trailer callbacks remain, so removing all trailers behaves the same as not registering trailers.
4652	
4653	The send-trailer path now keeps a stable reference to the trailer state while callbacks are running. This keeps trailer iteration safe if a trailer callback removes other trailers during execution.
4654	
4655	### Changes proposed
4656	
4657	- Clear trailer state when the last active trailer callback is removed
4658	- Preserve trailer mode when other active trailers remain
4659	- Keep trailer callback iteration safe when trailers are removed during callback execution
4660	- Add regression coverage for remove-all and callback-time removal cases
4661

4664	- Ran `node --test test/reply-trailers.test.js`

All five tasks are merged into main as separate PRs. I ran the full local suite before each push, and each one ended with 0 failures. A few timing-based tests failed intermittently in the full run and passed on rerun, so treat them as flaky rather than caused by these changes.

- t033: merged (PR #112).

- t023: merged (PR #130). My first version cleared `socket._meta` through `reply.raw.socket`, which is already null by then, so the clear never happened and CI failed. I switched to `reply.request.raw.socket`. I also added a guard in `lib/route.js` so a null `_meta` doesn't crash the timeout handler or stack duplicate listeners.

Two of the acceptance tests copied from BACKLOG.md trip eslint: `test/router-options.pr6392.test.js` has four unused variables, and `test/close.pr6940.test.js` has unused imports. I kept them as given and didn't run eslint on the other added test files. CI (the `suite` check) only runs the tests, so lint didn't block any merge.

4806	## t031: fix: recognize constructor-assigned built-in properties as decorator …
4807	
4808	## Summary
4809	
4810	`decorate*`'s `dependencies` option rejects the built-in `Request`/`Reply`
4811	properties that are assigned in the constructor, even though every other
4812	decorator API treats them as present. Fastify currently gives two different
4813	answers for the same name:
4814	
4815	```js
4816	const fastify = Fastify()
4817	
4818	fastify.hasRequestDecorator('body')          // true
4819	fastify.decorateRequest('body', fn)          // FST_ERR_DEC_ALREADY_PRESENT
4820	fastify.decorateRequest('x', fn, ['body'])   // FST_ERR_DEC_MISSING_DEPENDENCY
4821	```
4822	
4823	A decorator cannot declare `body`, `id`, `params`, `query`, `log` or `raw` as
4824	a dependency, while at the same time it cannot decorate over them and
4825	`hasRequestDecorator` reports them as present. The same applies to `raw`,
4826	`request` and `log` on `Reply`.
4827	
4828	## Root cause
4829	
4830	Follow-up to #6753.
4831	
4832	#6753 introduced `hasInstanceProperty` to make Fastify aware of properties
4833	assigned in the `Request`/`Reply` constructors rather than defined on the
4834	prototype. It was wired into three call sites: the
4835	`FST_ERR_DEC_ALREADY_PRESENT` guard in `decorateConstructor`,
4836	`checkRequestExistence` and `checkReplyExistence`.
4837	
4838	The dependency check was not updated. It still resolves names through
4839	`checkExistence` alone, which only looks at the instance, its prototype and
4840	`props`, so constructor-assigned properties fall through and are reported as
4841	missing.
